Lehi uses the phrase three times in five verses (15, 18, 19) as though it were the received scriptural name. It is instead the received *English* name, which by 1830 had been Milton's for a hundred and sixty years — “the Fruit / Of that Forbidden Tree” in the second line of Paradise Lost.
links.whyNot: Six KJV verses contain “the tree of life” and the identification rests on context rather than rarity; a reader could reasonably hold that Lehi is drawing on a general scriptural commonplace rather than Genesis 2:9 in particular.

pericopes.text: wherefore, the Lord God gave unto man, that he should act for himself. Wherefore, man could not act for himself, save it should be that he were enticed by the one or the other.

And I, Lehi, according to the things which I have read, must needs suppose, that an angel of God, according to that which is written, had fallen from Heaven; wherefore, he became a Devil, having sought that which was evil before God.

links.text: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!

provenance.other: Luke 10:18 (“I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven”) is the New Testament verse that made this reading standard, but it reads “fall” and not “fallen” and shares no other wording; the KJV form Lehi has is Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 14:12 is a taunt-song against the king of Babylon, and in Isaiah's own frame no angel falls in it; the Latin name Lucifer and the reading of the verse as Satan's fall are reception, not exegesis. Lehi does not read it as Isaiah wrote it — he reads it as the Christian tradition read it, and says he is doing so “according to that which is written.” The link records a case where what stands behind the Book of Mormon is not a biblical verse alone but a biblical verse's interpretive history. Isaiah 14 then brackets the whole discourse: its verse 12 opens Lehi's account of the devil here, and its verse 15 closes it at v. 29.

links.note: “Fallen from heaven” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Isaiah 14:12 and Job 1:16, where it is fire and not a person. Isaiah is the only candidate. What raises this above an ordinary allusion is that Lehi flags the citation himself — “according to the things which I have read … according to that which is written” — and this book transcribes Isaiah 14 in full at 2 Nephi 24, where verse 12 reads “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” The catalogue can therefore point to the text Lehi says he has read, inside the same book, in the same words.

pericopes.text: And because that he had fallen from Heaven, and had become miserable forever, he sought also the misery of all mankind.— Wherefore, he sayeth unto Eve, yea, even that old serpent, which is the Devil, which is the father of all lies; wherefore he sayeth, Partake of the forbidden fruit, and ye shall not die, but ye shall be as God, knowing good and evil.

links.text: And he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years,

provenance.other: Revelation 12:9, the only other KJV verse with the phrase, reads “called the Devil” and is displaced by a single word. The other epithet Lehi gives him in the same sentence, “the father of all lies,” occurs in no KJV verse at all; John 8:44 says only that the devil “is a liar, and the father of it.”
provenance.significance: Genesis 3 never says the serpent is the devil. Revelation is where the identification is made, and Lehi makes it in Revelation's exact words in the same sentence in which he quotes Genesis 3:4-5. So the Eden narrative reaches this chapter with its interpretation already attached: the words of the temptation are Genesis's, and the name of the tempter is the Apocalypse's. That is the chapter's demonology in one verse — an Old Testament story read through the last book of the New.

links.note: “That old serpent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, and the two are distinguished by one word: 12:9 reads “that old serpent, **called** the Devil,” 20:2 reads “that old serpent, **which is** the Devil.” Lehi has “that old serpent, which is the Devil.” Seven consecutive words from the later of the two, and the discrimination is decisive. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

links.text: And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:

provenance.other: 1830 reads “he sayeth unto Eve” where the KJV has “the serpent said unto the woman”; Genesis does not name her Eve until 3:20, after the expulsion sentence. Lehi names her at the temptation.
provenance.significance: “Ye shall be as gods” is the KJV's plural for a Hebrew word the same translators render “God” thousands of times, and Genesis 3:22 endorses the serpent on the point — “the man is become as one of us.” Lehi's singular closes that off: to be as God is one thing, definite, and the serpent's offer becomes a straightforward lie rather than a half-truth. The change is small, it is the kind of thing a translator's marginal alternative would license, and it converts the chapter's tempter into “the father of all lies” two clauses earlier.

links.note: “Ye shall not surely die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “knowing good and evil” in exactly one, Genesis 3:5. Lehi has the serpent's whole speech in order — “Partake of the forbidden fruit, and ye shall not die, but ye shall be as God, knowing good and evil” — with two departures that both matter. He drops “surely,” which is the word Genesis 3:4 uses to contradict God's “thou shalt surely die” of 2:17, so the retort loses its grip on the thing it retorts to. And he reads “as God” where the KJV reads “as gods,” singularising a plural the KJV had left standing. Nothing in Romans 5 or 1 Corinthians 15 reproduces any of this wording; the temptation reaches the Book of Mormon straight out of Genesis 3, unmediated.

pericopes.text: And after that Adam and Eve had partaken of the forbidden fruit, they were driven out from the garden of Eden, to till the earth.

links.text: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

provenance.other: “To till the ground” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 2:5 and 3:23. 1830 “driven out from the garden” → 1920 “of”.
provenance.significance: Genesis 3:23 sends Adam to till the ground “from whence he was taken” — the expulsion returns him to his own material, and the clause is a sentence of mortality. Lehi drops that clause and writes “to till the earth,” then immediately: “And they have brought forth children; yea, even the family of all the earth.” The word he substituted becomes the word the next verse turns on. Genesis's ground is what Adam is made of and goes back to; Lehi's earth is what gets populated. One noun changes the expulsion from a punishment into the beginning of a family.

links.note: Eight consecutive words, “from the garden of Eden, to till the,” and the highest n-gram score in the chapter. Lehi conflates the two halves of Genesis's expulsion: the verb is 3:24's (“So he drove out the man” — “they were driven out”), the destination and purpose are 3:23's. Two 1830 readings bear. The first edition reads “driven out **from** the garden of Eden,” which is Genesis 3:23's preposition; 1920 changed it to “of,” which is in neither Genesis verse — a later edition moving away from the source, and the borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the current text (CONVENTIONS §8). The second is Lehi's substantive change, kept in every edition: “to till the **earth**” for Genesis's “to till the ground.”

pericopes.text: And they have brought forth children; yea, even the family of all the earth.

And the days of the children of men were prolonged, according to the will of God, that they might repent while in the flesh; wherefore, their state became a state of probation, and their time was lengthened, according to the commandments which the Lord God gave unto the children of men. For he gave commandment that all men must repent; for he shewed unto all men that they were lost, because of the transgression of their parents.

And now, behold, if Adam had not transgressed, he would not have fallen; but he would have remained in the garden of Eden. And all things which were created, must have remained in the same state which they were, after that they were created; and they must have remained forever, and had no end.
And they would have had no children; wherefore, they would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery: doing no good, for they knew no sin.
But, behold, all things have been done in the wisdom of Him who knoweth all things.
Adam fell, that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.

links.text: For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 15:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon (form and doctrine, not wording)
provenance.other: Romans 5:12 (“by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin”) is the other candidate for the frame and shares no more wording than this one.
provenance.significance: Paul's antithesis makes Adam the entry of death and Christ the entry of life. Lehi keeps the form and reverses the valuation of its first member: Adam's fall is not what has to be undone but what makes there be anyone to redeem — “Adam fell, that men might be.” Set the two side by side and the Book of Mormon's most quoted sentence turns out to be 1 Corinthians 15:22 with the minus sign taken off Adam. The chapter has already prepared the reversal at vv. 22-23, where an unfallen Adam would have had no children and no joy; what is a catastrophe in Paul is a precondition in Lehi.

links.note: “Adam fell, that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy” shares with 1 Corinthians 15:22 exactly one word, Adam, and the entire shape of the sentence: a two-membered antithesis in which what Adam did is stated in order to be capped by what follows from it. This is the verse where the chapter's Pauline frame and its Genesis vocabulary finally have to be told apart, and the answer is that they never touch. Every phrase of Lehi's Eden — vv. 15, 18, 19, 22 — comes from the KJV of Genesis 2-3 with no New Testament wording anywhere in it, because neither Romans 5 nor 1 Corinthians 15 reproduces Genesis's language at all; and every doctrinal move Lehi makes about the fall comes from Paul with none of Genesis's wording. The two run in parallel through this chapter and are joined only here, in a sentence that has the wording of neither.
links.whyNot: One shared word. The link is asserted on the strength of a doctrinal argument's shape, and a reader who thinks Lehi reached this by reasoning from Genesis 3 alone has nothing in the verse to contradict him. It is recorded because the negative half of the finding — that no Pauline *wording* mediates the Eden material anywhere in this chapter — is worth stating at the verse where a reader would most expect it to.

pericopes.text: And the Messiah cometh in the fulness of time, that he might redeem the children of men from the fall. And because that they are redeemed from the fall, they have become free forever, knowing good from evil; to act for themselves, and not to be acted upon, save it be by the punishment of the law, at the great and last day, according to the commandments which God hath given.

Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which is expedient unto man. And they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great mediation of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the Devil: for he seeketh that all men might be miserable like unto himself.

links.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:

provenance.other: Deuteronomy 30:15 has the same figure with different pairs (“life and good, and death and evil”). “Eternal life” is not Deuteronomy's; Moses' life is “that both thou and thy seed may live” in the land, and the eschatological reading is imported.
provenance.significance: Moses calls heaven and earth to record because the choice he sets is one a nation makes once, in a land, with its length of days at stake. Lehi rescales it twice over: the choosing party becomes each man severally (“men are free according to the flesh”), and the stakes become eternal life and eternal death. The clause of Deuteronomy 30:19 he does not take is the one about seed and land. What survives the transfer is the bare structure of a set choice — which is exactly what the chapter needs, since a choice that is genuinely set before you is the practical form of “an opposition in all things.”

links.note: “Choose life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Lehi has Deuteronomy's whole structure: a choice set before the hearer, stated as two opposed pairs, with the imperative to choose the better — “free to choose liberty and eternal life … or to choose captivity and death.” Moses' pairs are life/death and blessing/cursing; Lehi's are liberty-and-eternal-life against captivity-and-death, which is Moses' first pair with the second collapsed into it. Hardy cross-references Deuteronomy 30:19 at v. 28, where the wording is only “choose eternal life”; the verbal contact is at v. 27, so the link sits here and the register sends a reader from 2:28 (CONVENTIONS §6a).

pericopes.text: And now, my sons, I would that ye should look to the great mediator, and hearken unto his great commandments; and be faithful unto his words, and choose eternal life, according to the will of his Holy Spirit,

links.text: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;

provenance.other: 1830 “the great mediation of all men” (2:27) → 1920 “the great Mediator of all men”. Hebrews' three uses attach the word to a covenant rather than to men.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 2:5's mediator is *one*, and the verse's force is exclusive — one God, one mediator, and no other. Lehi's is “the great mediator,” and he sets him against a rival: the devil of vv. 27 and 29, who also proposes a choice and also has power to captivate. The source verse's monotheistic arithmetic becomes, in Lehi, the ground of a two-sided choice, which the source verse does not offer and the chapter's whole doctrine of opposition requires.

links.note: “One mediator between God and men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “mediator” in the KJV is confined to it, to Galatians 3:19-20 (of Moses and the law) and to Hebrews 8:6, 9:15 and 12:24 (of the new covenant). Lehi's “the great mediator”, whom his sons are to look to and whose commandments they are to hearken to, is the Pauline figure and not the Mosaic one. The 1830 reading at v. 27 is the evidence that the term was under strain: the first edition prints “the great **mediation** of all men”, an abstract noun where the sense wants a person, and 1920 changed it to “Mediator” — moving the text toward 1 Timothy 2:5's noun (CONVENTIONS §8).
links.whyNot: The shared material is a single title. “Mediator” is the standard English theological term for the office by 1830 and is not confined to any one KJV verse's influence; the identification of 1 Timothy 2:5 in particular rests on the phrase's construction with “men”, which the 1830 text carries at v. 27 and the current text still does.

pericopes.text: and not choose eternal death, according to the will of the flesh and the evil which is therein, which giveth the spirit of the Devil power to captivate, to bring you down to hell, that he may reign over you in his own kingdom.

links.text: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

provenance.significance: John 1:13 is about how one comes to be a child of God: not by any human willing. Lehi's sentence is about how one comes to be the devil's: by one's own willing. Recovering the source turns the borrowing into a deliberate asymmetry — the will of the flesh cannot produce the new birth but is entirely sufficient to produce the captivity. Lehi has taken the one thing John says human will cannot do and named the one thing it can.

links.note: “The will of the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Lehi opposes it to “the will of his Holy Spirit” in the preceding clause, and the pairing of a fleshly will against a divine one is John 1:13's own construction — born “not of the will of the flesh … but of God.” This is the second of two links in this chapter to consecutive verses of the Johannine prologue; John 1:14 stands behind 2:6.

links.text: Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

provenance.alternative: Matthew 11:23 has the identical clause; mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, and the case for Isaiah rests on recurrence within the discourse rather than on wording.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 14 brackets Lehi's account of the devil. Verse 12 opens it — the angel “fallen from Heaven” at 2:17 — and verse 15 closes it here, thirteen verses later. But the two ends are not used the same way. In Isaiah, being brought down to hell is what happens *to* Lucifer; in Lehi it is what Lucifer does to you, “that he may reign over you in his own kingdom.” The taunt-song's sentence on the tyrant becomes the tyrant's own instrument, and the kingdom Isaiah's king lost is the kingdom Lehi's devil rules.

links.note: “Brought down to hell” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 14:15 and Matthew 11:23, which is Christ applying Isaiah's taunt to Capernaum. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between them at any point Lehi reproduces, so this verse cannot settle its own source on wording. Recurrence settles it instead: Lehi has already quoted Isaiah 14:12 at v. 17, naming it as something he has read, and this book transcribes the whole chapter at 2 Nephi 24. Isaiah 14 is a text demonstrably in front of him; Matthew is not established anywhere in the discourse.
links.whyNot: No wording distinguishes Isaiah 14:15 from Matthew 11:23 here, and the argument is entirely one of which text the discourse has established. A reader who declines the recurrence argument is left with a genuine two-way tie.

pericopes.text: I have spoken these few words unto you all, my sons, in the last days of my probation; and I have chosen the good part, according to the words of the prophet. And I have none other object, save it be the everlasting welfare of your souls.— Amen.

links.text: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.

provenance.other: The attribution formula is Lehi's own; the KJV contains no prophetic saying about a good part. See CONVENTIONS §3a on availability: the anachronism is the finding, not an objection to it.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's purest instance of the inverted availability criterion, and it is worth the whole verse. Recover Luke 10:42 and what Mary chose was to sit at Jesus' feet and hear his word instead of serving — and Lehi, in the last days of his probation, says he has chosen it, at the end of a chapter in which he has done nothing but talk while his sons sat and listened. The commendation of hearing over doing is spoken by a dying man to the sons who must now do. Luke's next clause, “which shall not be taken away from her,” is answered in Lehi's next: “the everlasting welfare of your souls.” Neither text says any of this. The link says it — and it says it on a saying that, on the book's own chronology, no one had yet spoken.

links.note: “Good part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the phrase there is “chosen that good part” — the whole of Lehi's “I have chosen the good part,” with the demonstrative traded for an article. Four words from a singleton, in the same construction with the same verb. What makes the row is the clause Lehi attaches to it: “according to the words of the prophet.” The words are not a prophet's. They are Jesus' at Bethany, about Mary, in a Gospel, and no prophet in the KJV says anything of the kind.

pericopes.text: And now I speak unto you, Joseph, my last born. Thou wast born in the wilderness of mine afflictions; yea, in the days of my greatest sorrow, did thy mother bear thee.

provenance.other: 'Last born' occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's word for this position is 'youngest', which it uses seventeen times, ten of them of Benjamin in Genesis 42-44. 'Son of my sorrow' is likewise absent, being the KJV's marginal gloss on Benoni rather than its text.
provenance.significance: Lehi has been playing Jacob since 2 Nephi 1, and the sequence of blessings ends where Jacob's family began: with a last son borne in his mother's extremity. In Genesis the child of that labour is named twice over, Benoni by the dying mother and Benjamin by the father, and the second name cancels the first - sorrow renamed as the right hand. 2 Nephi 3 does the same operation with the other name from Rachel's two sons: the last-born of the affliction is called Joseph, and the whole chapter that follows is an argument that the name is a promise. Lehi's two youngest are Jacob and Joseph, which puts Rachel's grandson's name on the elder and her son's on the younger; the naming runs backwards through Genesis, and the chapter's business is to make that name do work.

links.note: 'Thou wast born in the wilderness of mine afflictions; yea, in the days of my greatest sorrow, did thy mother bear thee.' There is almost no shared wording here and the link is offered as form, not diction: the KJV has one birth answering this description, Rachel's at Genesis 35:16-18, where a last son is borne in hard labour on a journey and named for his mother's sorrow. The chapter that follows is entirely about what a name inherited from Joseph obliges, so a first verse shaped by the KJV's one naming-in-sorrow is doing more than setting a scene. Note that the tie is to the wrong son of Rachel - the Genesis scene produces Benjamin, and Lehi's verse produces Joseph - which is why this is filed as figural and at moderate rather than higher.
links.whyNot: No phrase of Genesis 35:16-18 survives into 2 Nephi 3:1. 'Last born', 'wilderness of mine afflictions' and 'my greatest sorrow' are all outside the KJV's vocabulary for this scene, and a reader who wants the resemblance to be nothing more than the common circumstance of a youngest child born in hardship can have that reading; nothing in the wording forbids it.
links.text: And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.

pericopes.text: And may the Lord consecrate also unto thee this land, which is a most precious land for thine inheritance and the inheritance of thy seed with thy brethren, for thy security forever, if it so be that ye shall keep the commandments of the Holy One of Israel.
And now, Joseph, my last born, whom I have brought out of the wilderness of mine afflictions, may the Lord bless thee forever, for thy seed shall not utterly be destroyed.
For behold, thou art the fruit of my loins; and I am a descendant of Joseph, which was carried captive into Egypt. And great was the covenants of the Lord, which he made unto Joseph;

wherefore, Joseph truly saw our day. And he obtained a promise of the Lord, that out of the fruit of his loins, the Lord God would raise up a righteous branch unto the House of Israel; not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off; nevertheless, to be remembered in the covenants of the Lord, that the Messiah should be made manifest unto them in the latter days, in the spirit of power, unto the bringing of them out of darkness unto light; yea, out of hidden darkness and out of captivity unto freedom.

provenance.route: Psalm 132:11 -> Acts 2:30 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Psalm 132:11 - 'The LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy BODY will I set upon thy throne.' Acts 2:30 quotes this verse and renders it 'of the fruit of his LOINS'.
provenance.other: 'Fruit of his loins' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:30, and 'fruit of thy loins' in none. The refrain that organizes this whole chapter therefore has one biblical parent, and it is a New Testament one.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:30 is Peter at Pentecost, and it says that God swore to David that of the fruit of his loins he would raise up Christ. 2 Nephi 3:5 takes that sentence entire - the fruit of his loins, the raising up, the sworn promise - and then, in the same breath, refuses its predicate: 'not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off.' The one KJV verse in which a promise about the fruit of a patriarch's loins produces the Messiah is the verse this chapter borrows in order to promise something else. The metalepsis is exact and it is a disavowal: recover Acts 2:30's context and the disclaimer 'not the Messiah' turns out to be answering the source rather than merely qualifying the claim. The phrase then repeats twenty-odd times in twenty-five verses, so the whole chapter is spoken in a diction that arrives from Peter's Pentecost sermon.

links.note: 'And he obtained a promise of the Lord, that out of the fruit of his loins, the Lord God would raise up a righteous branch unto the House of Israel; not the Messiah.' Two elements of Acts 2:30 stand together here in Acts's order: 'of the fruit of his loins' - a KJV singleton - and 'he would raise up'. Acts supplies the syntax of a sworn dynastic promise fulfilled in an offspring raised up out of a named ancestor's loins, and 2 Nephi 3 keeps the frame while changing the referent from Christ to a branch. The borrowing is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his long quotations; its force is rarity, not length.
links.text: Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;

provenance.other: 'Righteous Branch' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jeremiah 33:15 has the same figure in the other order, 'the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David'; no other verse joins the adjective to the noun.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 23:5's righteous Branch is raised unto David and is a king who reigns; it is one of the Old Testament's principal messianic texts and was read as such throughout the Christian tradition. 2 Nephi 3:5 borrows the phrase and immediately withholds the identification - 'not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off' - so the verse is built out of two of the most explicitly messianic sentences in the KJV, Acts 2:30 and Jeremiah 23:5, and spends its second half denying that it means what they mean. That double borrowing-and-refusal is the verse's whole rhetorical shape.

links.note: 'The Lord God would raise up a righteous branch unto the House of Israel.' Jeremiah 23:5 is the KJV's one 'righteous Branch', and it is raised up, as here. The substitution is the argument: Jeremiah raises the Branch unto David, 2 Nephi raises it unto the house of Israel, and the messianic sense that attaches to the phrase everywhere else is then explicitly declined. Lehi is speaking a few years after Jeremiah on the book's own chronology, which makes this the rare case where an availability objection does not arise; what remains a finding is that the wording is the KJV's English and not a translator's independent choice.
links.text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

provenance.other: 'Broken off' occurs in five KJV verses; three are Romans 11:17, 19 and 20, all of branches broken from the olive tree, and one is Isaiah 27:11, of withered boughs. Genesis 49:22, the blessing this chapter is expounding, calls Joseph 'a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall'.
provenance.significance: A branch that is broken off yet remembered in the covenant is Romans 11's argument in miniature - the natural branches broken off, and God able to graff them in again. What the Book of Mormon does with it is unusual: in Romans the branches are broken off for unbelief and their breaking is a warning, while here the breaking is the promise itself, the mechanism by which Joseph's seed is carried away and preserved. The figure is inverted rather than borrowed.

links.note: 'A branch which was to be broken off; nevertheless, to be remembered in the covenants of the Lord.' The verbal contact is two words, and they are the two words Romans 11 uses three times for the severed branches of Israel. The reason for recording it at moderate rather than dismissing it is context: this clause sits between a messianic Branch drawn from Jeremiah 23:5 and a covenant-remembrance, which is precisely Romans 11's subject matter, and the chapter being expounded calls Joseph a bough with branches. Genesis supplies the image, Romans the verb.
links.whyNot: 'Broken off' is ordinary English and Romans 11's sense is the reverse of this verse's: there the branches are broken off in judgment, here in promise. A reader may reasonably hold that the Book of Mormon has simply continued Genesis 49:22's arboreal figure without any New Testament help.
links.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

pericopes.text: For Joseph truly testified, saying: A seer shall the Lord my God raise up, which shall be a choice seer unto the fruit of my loins.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15 -> Acts 3:22 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 18:15 - 'The LORD THY God WILL RAISE UP UNTO THEE A PROPHET from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken.'
provenance.other: 'Truly said' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:22 ('For Moses truly said unto the fathers'). Acts 7:37, the only other place the Deuteronomy 18 prophecy is quoted, reads 'which said unto the children of Israel' and has no 'truly'. The three occurrences of the formula in this chapter - 'Joseph truly saw our day' (3:5), 'For Joseph truly testified, saying' (3:6), 'Yea, Joseph truly said' (3:7) - therefore all track Acts 3:22 and not Acts 7:37.
provenance.significance: Two things arrive together and they arrive from the same verse. First the citation formula: Acts 3:22 is the KJV's only 'X truly said', and 2 Nephi 3 uses it three times in three verses with Joseph substituted for Moses. Second the syntax: Deuteronomy 18:15 is subject-first, 'The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet'; Acts 3:22 fronts the object, 'A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you'; and 2 Nephi 3:6 reads 'A seer shall the Lord my God raise up'. The inversion is Peter's, not Moses's. Recover the context and the substitution is the finding: Peter at Solomon's porch is arguing that Deuteronomy's prophet-like-Moses is Jesus, and 2 Nephi 3 lifts both his formula and his word order in order to make Joseph the prophesier and a seer, not a prophet, the thing prophesied. The chapter thereby claims the Book of Mormon's own authorizing text in the very sentence Peter used to claim it for Christ.

links.note: 'For Joseph truly testified, saying: A seer shall the Lord my God raise up, which shall be a choice seer unto the fruit of my loins.' This is Acts 3:22 with three substitutions and no change of shape: 'Joseph truly testified' for 'Moses truly said', 'a seer' for 'a prophet', 'my God' for 'your God'. Deuteronomy 18:15 cannot be the proximate source, because Deuteronomy neither inverts the clause nor has 'truly'; both belong to Peter's quotation of it. 1 Nephi 22:20 already reproduced twenty-six continuous words of this same verse, so the Book of Mormon has been working from Acts 3:22 rather than Deuteronomy 18 since the first book - what 2 Nephi 3 adds is the redeployment of the formula onto Joseph. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold: the run here is six words, and the case rests on the inversion and the singleton 'truly said'.
links.text: For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.

pericopes.text: Yea, Joseph truly said, thus saith the Lord unto me: A choice seer will I raise up out of the fruit of thy loins; and he shall be esteemed highly among the fruit of thy loins. And unto him will I give commandment, that he shall do a work for the fruit of thy loins, his brethren, which shall be of great worth unto them, even to the bringing of them to the knowledge of the covenants which I have made with thy fathers.
And I will give unto him a commandment, that he shall do none other work, save the work which I shall command him. And I will make him great in mine eyes: for he shall do my work.
And he shall be great like unto Moses, whom I have said I would raise up unto you, to deliver my people, O house of Israel.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15 -> Acts 3:22 / Acts 7:37 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 18:15 reads 'raise up UNTO THEE a Prophet'; Deuteronomy 18:18, 'I will raise THEM up a Prophet from among their brethren, LIKE UNTO THEE'.
provenance.other: 'Raise up unto you' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 3:22 and Acts 7:37, and in neither of the Deuteronomy verses they quote. 'Raise up unto thee' occurs in exactly one, Deuteronomy 18:15. 2 Nephi 3:9 has the Acts form.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation test decided on a single pronoun. Deuteronomy addresses Israel as 'thee'; Acts, quoting it to a crowd, has 'unto you'; and 2 Nephi 3:9 - 'whom I have said I would raise up unto you' - takes the plural. The verse also converts Acts's 'like unto me', spoken by Moses of a coming prophet, into 'like unto Moses', spoken of a coming seer, which turns Peter's comparison inside out: in Acts the point is that the new figure resembles Moses, and here the point is that the new figure resembles Moses while explicitly not being the prophet Moses foretold. The chapter is running Deuteronomy 18 through Acts and then diverting it from the Messiah to the seer.

links.note: 'And he shall be great like unto Moses, whom I have said I would raise up unto you, to deliver my people, O house of Israel.' Three words settle the route. 'Raise up unto you' is Acts's; Deuteronomy 18:15 reads 'unto thee' and is the only KJV verse that does. Having established the seer at 3:6 in Acts 3:22's inverted syntax, the chapter now measures him against Moses in Acts 3:22's pronoun. The clause 'to deliver my people' is not in either source and comes from the Exodus material that governs 3:10 and 3:17.
links.text: For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.

pericopes.text: And Moses will I raise up, to deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt.

provenance.other: 'Out of the land of Egypt' occurs in eighty-one KJV verses and identifies nothing on its own; the rarity here is zero and the link rests entirely on the commissioning scene. Exodus 3:8 has 'to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians', which is the KJV's nearest use of 'deliver' for this act.
provenance.significance: Where the chapter's other Moses material is verbally precise, this verse is not, and saying so matters: 2 Nephi 3:10 is the one sentence in the passage that could have been written by anyone who knew the story at second hand. Its function is structural rather than allusive - it holds the place of the first Moses so that 3:11 can set the seer beside him.

links.note: 'And Moses will I raise up, to deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt.' The commissioning of Moses in Exodus 3 is unmistakably in view, but nothing in the wording is distinctive: every content word here is KJV commonplace, and 'out of the land of Egypt' appears in eighty-one verses. The link is recorded because the verse is doing real work in the argument - it supplies the Moses whom 3:9 has just invoked and 3:17 will rewrite - not because the diction points anywhere in particular.
links.text: Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.

pericopes.text: But a seer will I raise up out of the fruit of thy loins; and unto him will I give power to bring forth my word unto the seed of thy loins; and not to the bringing forth my word only, saith the Lord, but to the convincing them of my word, which shall have already gone forth among them.

Wherefore, the fruit of my loins shall write; and the fruit of the loins of Judah shall write; and that which shall be written by the fruit of thy loins, and also that which shall be written by the fruit of the loins of Judah, shall grow together, unto the confounding of false doctrines, and laying down of contentions, and establishing peace among the fruit of thy loins, and bringing them to the knowledge of their fathers in the latter days; and also to the knowledge of my covenants, saith the Lord.

provenance.other: 'The stick of Joseph' and 'shall be one in mine hand' are each KJV singletons, both in Ezekiel 37:19. Ezekiel 37:16 is the only KJV verse that commands writing upon a thing for Judah and writing upon another thing for Joseph.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 37:16-19 is the only place in the Bible where a record for Judah and a record for Joseph are made and then joined, and 2 Nephi 3:12 is that passage with one substitution: sticks become writings. The substitution is itself an interpretation, and it is the interpretation on which the Book of Mormon's account of its own status depends - the book is the stick of Joseph, the Bible the stick of Judah, and their joining in Ezekiel's hand becomes their growing together on the page. What Ezekiel does not supply is the purpose clause. In Ezekiel the two sticks are joined to end the division of the kingdoms; here they are joined 'unto the confounding of false doctrines, and laying down of contentions, and establishing peace', which is a controversy about doctrine and not a reunion of tribes. The source is transposed from politics to polemic.

links.note: 'The fruit of my loins shall write; and the fruit of the loins of Judah shall write; and that which shall be written by the fruit of thy loins, and also that which shall be written by the fruit of the loins of Judah, shall grow together.' Judah and Joseph, each with a written thing, brought into one: there is one such passage in the KJV. The shared vocabulary is thin - 'write', 'Judah', 'Joseph' - and the machine streams did not propose it, because the agreement is with a sequence of images across four verses rather than with any contiguous run of words. That is exactly the blindness CONVENTIONS section 9 describes. Confidence is high on the strength of the configuration; kjvSpecific is left uncertain because no phrase of Ezekiel's English survives to be tested.
links.text: Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand.

provenance.other: 'Grow together' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:30, in the parable of the tares: 'Let both grow together until the harvest.'
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 37:19 says the two sticks 'shall be one in mine hand'. 2 Nephi 3:12 declines that verb and reaches instead for the KJV's one instance of 'grow together', which belongs to the wheat and the tares. The consequence is that the sentence describing the union of two true records is worded out of the parable about the coexistence of the true crop and the false one until they are separated by fire - and the very next clause is 'unto the confounding of false doctrines'. Whether that is design or diction, the catalogue's business is to record that the phrase has one home in the KJV and that its home is a parable about telling the false from the true.

links.note: Recorded because 'grow together' is a KJV singleton and the writer's English has to come from somewhere; the substitution of it for Ezekiel's 'shall be one in mine hand' is a real choice at a load-bearing point in the sentence. The catalogue takes the risk of proposing it under CONVENTIONS section 0a rather than filing it as a coincidence.
links.whyNot: The senses are not merely different but nearly opposed. Matthew 13:30 lets wheat and tares grow together precisely so that they may be separated at harvest; 2 Nephi 3:12 has two records grow together into one testimony. Nothing else of the parable is present - no harvest, no tares, no reapers - and 'grow together' is available as ordinary English without any parable behind it. A cautious reader should decline this link, and the exclusion register would have been the other defensible home for it.
links.text: Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.

pericopes.text: And out of weakness he shall be made strong, in that day when my work shall commence among all my people, unto the restoring thee, O house of Israel, saith the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Out of weakness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the full clause 'out of weakness were made strong' likewise. Both are Hebrews 11:34.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:34 is in the roll of the faithful, and the men it describes as made strong out of weakness are judges and warriors who by faith 'waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens'. 2 Nephi 3:13 applies the clause to a seer whose strength is a book, and 3:21 completes the transfer - 'the weakness of their words will I make strong in their faith' - so that Hebrews' martial vocabulary of strength out of weakness is spent entirely on writing and reading. The metalepsis is the pivot: recover Hebrews 11 and the whole point of the chapter is that faith is what turns the weak into the strong, which is exactly the warrant 2 Nephi 3:19-21 needs for a record that speaks 'according to the simpleness of their words'. 1 Nephi 4:2 already drew on Hebrews 11:29, so this is the same chapter of Hebrews being worked a second time.

links.note: 'And out of weakness he shall be made strong.' Seven words against the KJV's 'out of weakness were made strong', with the tense and number adjusted to a single future figure. The phrase exists nowhere else in the Bible. This is short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his long quotations; it is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton, on the same principle as 1 Nephi 1:14.
links.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

pericopes.text: And thus prophesied Joseph, saying: Behold, that seer will the Lord bless; and they that seek to destroy him, shall be confounded: for this promise, of which I have obtained of the Lord, of the fruit of thy loins, shall be fulfilled. Behold, I am sure of the fulfilling of this promise.

And his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father. And he shall be like unto me; for the thing which the Lord shall bring forth by his hand, by the power of the Lord shall bring my people unto salvation;

provenance.other: 'After the name of his father' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:59. No other verse in the Bible names a child after his father in those words.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:59-61 is the KJV's one scene of naming a son after his father, and it is a scene in which the naming is refused: they would have called him Zacharias after the name of his father, and his mother said 'Not so; but he shall be called John', and the neighbours objected that there is none of thy kindred that is called by this name. 2 Nephi 3:15 asserts, of the promised seer, exactly what Luke 1 denies of the forerunner - 'his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father'. Recover the context and the borrowing turns into a reversal: the words that in the KJV introduce a broken naming-custom are used here to guarantee an unbroken one. The pairing with 3:24's 'great in the sight of God', which is Luke 1:15's singleton phrase about the same child, means the chapter's closing description of the latter-day figure is assembled out of the KJV's account of John the Baptist.

links.note: 'And his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father.' The second clause is Luke 1:59 word for word, and it is the only place those words stand in the KJV. The first clause reaches the other way, to Genesis 48:6's 'shall be called after' - see the separate row - so the sentence fuses the KJV's two singleton naming formulae, one from the Joseph blessing this chapter is expounding and one from the naming of John. The machine stream proposed both verses and ranked Lamentations 1:21 above them; see the exclusion register.
links.text: And it came to pass, that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child; and they called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.

provenance.other: 'Shall be called after' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 48:6. Genesis 48:16, four verses further on, has Jacob's 'let my name be named on them' over Joseph's sons.
provenance.significance: Genesis 48 is Jacob adopting Joseph's two sons and ruling how the later issue shall be named, and Genesis 48:16 asks that his own name be named on them. 2 Nephi 3 is Lehi doing the same thing at the end of his life to his own last son, and 3:15's promise that a descendant's name shall be called after Joseph's is Genesis 48's naming provision projected forward. The chapter is not alluding to Genesis 48 in passing; it is performing it.

links.note: 'His name shall be called after me.' Four words that stand in one KJV verse, and that verse is in the chapter immediately before the Joseph blessing this passage expounds. The confidence is moderate rather than high because 'shall be called after' is unremarkable English and Genesis 48:6's clause continues 'the name of their brethren in their inheritance', which the Book of Mormon does not take; what raises it above a coincidence is that the whole speech is a deathbed disposition of Joseph's inheritance, which is Genesis 48's subject.
links.text: And thy issue, which thou begettest after them, shall be thine, and shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.

pericopes.text: yea, thus prophesied Joseph. I am sure of this thing, even as I am sure of the promise of Moses: for the Lord hath said unto me, I will preserve thy seed forever.

provenance.other: 'Preserve you a posterity' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:7; 'to preserve' in only two, Genesis 45:5 and 45:7, both in the same speech.
provenance.significance: The KJV's language of preserving a seed belongs to Joseph in Egypt and to almost no one else: it is what he says to his brothers when he discloses himself, that God sent him before them to preserve a posterity in the earth. 2 Nephi 3 puts that sentence in the Lord's mouth as a promise made to Joseph rather than an explanation offered by him - 'I will preserve thy seed forever' - and the chapter's two other promises of non-destruction (3:3, 3:23) run on the same idea. The chapter is thus quoting Joseph's own theology of his exile back at his descendants: the preservation that Genesis 45 explains retrospectively is here guaranteed in advance.

links.note: 'For the Lord hath said unto me, I will preserve thy seed forever.' Only 'preserve' and the idea of a seed survive verbally, and 'preserve' with a posterity as its object is nearly confined in the KJV to Genesis 45:5-7. The link is at moderate: the wording is too thin to prove dependence, but the sentence is a compressed statement of the one speech in the Bible where Joseph accounts for his own captivity as the preserving of a seed, and this chapter is about nothing else.
links.whyNot: Nothing but a single common verb is shared. A reader may hold that 'I will preserve thy seed' needs no source at all, and the covenant language of Genesis 17 or 2 Samuel 7 would serve the sense equally.
links.text: And God sent me before you to preserve you a posterity in the earth, and to save your lives by a great deliverance.

pericopes.text: And the Lord hath said, I will raise up a Moses; and I will give power unto him in a rod; and I will give judgment unto him in writing. Yet I will not loose his tongue, that he shall speak much: for I will not make him mighty in speaking. But I will write unto him my law, by the finger of mine own hand; and I will make a spokesman for him.

provenance.route: Exodus 4:10-17 (with Exodus 31:18) -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Spokesman' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 4:16. 'Slow of speech' and 'not eloquent' are each singletons at Exodus 4:10, and 'take this rod' a singleton at Exodus 4:17. 'Written with the finger' occurs in two verses, Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10.
provenance.significance: Every element of this verse is drawn from one page of Exodus, and taken together they reproduce the whole logic of Moses's commissioning: the rod that does signs, the mouth that cannot speak, the brother appointed as spokesman, and the law written by God's own finger. What the Book of Mormon changes is the answer to the objection. In Exodus, Moses pleads that he is slow of speech and God replies 'I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say' (4:12), giving Aaron only as a concession. In 2 Nephi 3:17 the Lord makes the disability a decree - 'I will not loose his tongue, that he shall speak much: for I will not make him mighty in speaking' - and the spokesman is not a concession but the design. The metalepsis runs against the source: recover Exodus 4 and this verse is God refusing to do for the latter-day Moses what he offered to do for the first.
provenance.alternative: Mark 7:35, 'the string of his tongue was loosed', is the KJV's only loosing of a tongue and may stand behind 'I will not loose his tongue'; it is recorded here rather than as a separate row because the surrounding sentence is Exodus 4 throughout and Mark supplies at most one verb.

links.note: 'I will give power unto him in a rod; and I will give judgment unto him in writing. Yet I will not loose his tongue, that he shall speak much: for I will not make him mighty in speaking. But I will write unto him my law, by the finger of mine own hand; and I will make a spokesman for him.' Four singletons of Exodus 4 and one of Exodus 31 stand in five clauses: the rod of 4:17, the impeded speech of 4:10, the spokesman of 4:16 - a word found nowhere else in the KJV - and the finger that writes the law of 31:18. The machine's top candidate for this verse was Revelation 11:3 on the run 'and I will give power unto'; see the exclusion register. Note also that the verse denies of its Moses exactly what Acts 7:22 asserts of the first one, that he 'was mighty in words and in deeds'; the reply comes at 3:24.
links.text: And he shall be thy spokesman unto the people: and he shall be, even he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God.

pericopes.text: And the Lord said unto me also, I will raise up unto the fruit of thy loins; and I will make for him a spokesman. And I, behold, I will give unto him, that he shall write the writing of the fruit of thy loins, unto the fruit of thy loins; and the spokesman of thy loins shall declare it.

And the words which he shall write, shall be the words which is expedient in my wisdom, should go forth unto the fruit of thy loins. And it shall be as if the fruit of thy loins had cried unto them from the dust: for I know their faith.

provenance.other: 'Whisper out of the dust' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Out of the dust' occurs in five, of which Isaiah 29:4 is the only one in which anything speaks from it; the other four raise the poor out of it or wash things from it. 'From the dust' is a singleton at Isaiah 52:2, but there it is dust to be shaken off - see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:4 is a threat: Ariel is brought down, and her speech comes low out of the dust like a familiar spirit's, the voice of a city reduced to a ghost. 2 Nephi 3:19 takes that image and makes it a promise - a buried people crying repentance to their brethren out of the ground - so a prophecy of humiliation becomes a prophecy of publication. The transformation is the whole argument of 2 Nephi 26-27, where Isaiah 29 is expanded at length and the speech from the dust is identified with the book itself; 3:19 is where the reading enters the text, six chapters before the exposition that will defend it. Note the necromantic register Isaiah supplies and the Book of Mormon does not repeat: 'as of one that hath a familiar spirit' is left behind, which is a discriminating omission, since a record speaking from the earth is otherwise open to precisely that charge.

links.note: 'And it shall be as if the fruit of thy loins had cried unto them from the dust: for I know their faith.' The KJV has one passage in which speech comes out of the dust, and this is a paraphrase of it rather than a quotation - the borrowed element is the image plus the preposition, not a run of words. 'Cried' replaces Isaiah's 'whisper' and 'be low', which raises the volume of the source considerably and is consistent with the use the chapter is making of it. 3:20 continues the figure: 'And they shall cry from the dust'.
links.text: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.

pericopes.text: And they shall cry from the dust; yea, even repentance unto their brethren, even that after many generations have gone by them. And it shall come to pass that their cry shall go, even according to the simpleness of their words.

Because of their faith, their words shall proceed forth out of my mouth unto their brethren, which are the fruit of thy loins; and the weakness of their words will I make strong in their faith, unto the remembering of my covenant which I made unto thy fathers.
And now, behold, my son Joseph, after this manner did my father of old prophesy.
Wherefore, because of this covenant, thou art blessed: for thy seed shall not be destroyed, for they shall hearken unto the words of the Book.

And there shall raise up one, mighty among them, which shall do much good, both in word and in deed, being an instrument in the hands of God, with exceeding faith, to work mighty wonders, and do that thing which is great in the sight of God, unto the bringing to pass much restoration unto the House of Israel, and unto the seed of thy brethren.

provenance.other: “mighty in” occurs in exactly 13 KJV verses, but only two of them join words to deeds: Acts 7:22, of Moses ('mighty in words and in deeds'), and Luke 24:19, of Jesus ('a prophet mighty in deed and word'). The Book of Mormon's own order, “in word and in deed”, occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, so the borrowing is of the collocation and not of a run.
provenance.significance: Acts 7:22 is Stephen's Moses, mighty in words and in deeds - a description Exodus 4:10 flatly contradicts, since the Moses of Exodus is not eloquent and is slow of speech. 2 Nephi 3 has already taken Stephen's side of that contradiction apart at 3:17, where the Lord declares that he will not make the latter-day Moses 'mighty in speaking'. Seven verses later a different figure appears who is 'mighty among them, which shall do much good, both in word and in deed'. The chapter has distributed Acts 7:22 across two people: the seer gets the deeds and the writing and is denied the words, and this one gets both. Stephen's sermon is also where Deuteronomy 18's prophecy stands at 7:37, so the chapter's Moses material and its 'mighty in word and deed' material come from the same fifteen verses of Acts.

links.note: 'And there shall raise up one, mighty among them, which shall do much good, both in word and in deed.' The pairing of might in word with might in deed is Acts 7:22's formula for Moses, which matters here because this chapter is an argument about a second Moses and has just spent 3:17 denying him one half of it. The link is at moderate: the phrase order differs from both New Testament verses and the elements are ordinary, so the case rests on the collocation and on the chapter's demonstrable interest in Stephen's Moses.
links.whyNot: 'Word and deed' is a commonplace of English devotional prose independent of any verse, and neither Acts 7:22 nor Luke 24:19 is reproduced in order or wording. A reader may take the resemblance as idiom rather than allusion.
links.text: And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.

provenance.other: 'Great in the sight' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:15, of John the Baptist: 'For he shall be great in the sight of the Lord.' The Book of Mormon has 'great in the sight of God' rather than 'of the Lord'.
provenance.significance: Taken with 3:15, this is the second singleton from Luke 1 in one chapter, and both belong to the same episode - the annunciation and naming of John. Luke 1:15 promises that the forerunner shall be great in the sight of the Lord; Luke 1:59 records the attempt to name him after his father. 2 Nephi 3 takes the first for its final figure and the second for its seer, so the chapter's account of the latter-day instruments is worded, at two of its most emphatic points, out of the KJV's account of the man sent to prepare the way. That is a coherent choice of source for a chapter about forerunners, and it is worth naming even though neither borrowing is long.

links.note: 'And do that thing which is great in the sight of God.' Four words that stand in one KJV verse, with 'God' for 'the Lord'. Compare 3:8's 'I will make him great in mine eyes', which reaches for the same idea without the phrase. The machine's top proposal for this verse was Luke 12:26's 'do that thing which is least'; the shared run is longer and the sense is the opposite, and it is filed in the exclusion register.
links.whyNot: The substitution of 'God' for 'the Lord' breaks the run, and greatness in God's sight is an unremarkable thing to say. A reader may reasonably hold that the four-word agreement is coincidence rather than borrowing.
links.text: For he shall be great in the sight of the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother’s womb.

pericopes.text: And now, blessed art thou, Joseph. Behold, thou art little; wherefore, hearken unto the words of thy brother Nephi, and it shall be done unto thee, even according to the words which I have spoken. Remember the words of thy dying father. Amen.
And now, I, Nephi, speak concerning the prophecies of which my father hath spoken, concerning Joseph, who was carried into Egypt:

For behold, he truly prophesied concerning all his seed. And the prophecies which he wrote, there are not many greater. And he prophesied concerning us, and our future generations; and they are written upon the plates of brass.

Wherefore, after my father had made an end of speaking concerning the prophecies of Joseph, he called the children of Laman, his sons, and his daughters, and sayeth unto them, Behold, my sons, and my daughters, which are the sons and the daughters of my first born, I would that ye should give ear unto my words:
for the Lord God hath said, That inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; and inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall be cut off from my presence.

links.text: Say unto them, Whosoever he be of all your seed among your generations, that goeth unto the holy things, which the children of Israel hallow unto the LORD, having his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.

provenance.other: “cut off from my presence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 22:3. The Book of Mormon's own covenant formula elsewhere reads otherwise — 1 Nephi 2:21 has “cut off from the presence of the Lord” — so the Levitical wording enters here and not at the formula's first statement.
provenance.significance: The promise half of the covenant (“ye shall prosper in the land”) has no KJV phrase behind it at all; the threat half does, and it is a purity law. Leviticus 22:3 cuts off a priest who approaches the holy things with uncleanness upon him. Lehi's grandchildren are not priests and the sanction is territorial, not cultic — but the sentence that carries God's severity into the Book of Mormon's central covenant is a sentence about a man barred from the altar.

links.note: Lehi states the land-covenant in its standard Book of Mormon form, and the negative clause departs from the form used at its first statement. 1 Nephi 2:21 and 1 Nephi 4:14 have “the presence of the Lord”; 2 Nephi 4:4 has “from my presence”, first person, which is Leviticus 22:3's phrasing and no other KJV verse's. The positive clause has no KJV parallel — “prosper in the land” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses — so the borrowing is one-sided: the blessing is the book's own idiom and the curse is the King James Bible's.

pericopes.text: But behold, my sons and my daughters, I cannot go down to my grave, save I should leave a blessing upon you: For behold, I know that if ye are brought up in the right way that ye should go, ye will not depart from it.

links.text: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.

provenance.other: Both halves are KJV singletons: “in the way he should go” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “will not depart from it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 22:6 is a maxim about the durability of early training; Lehi turns it into a warrant for a deathbed blessing that will outlive him, and immediately extends it past the child to the grandchild — “that the cursing may be taken from you, and be answered upon the heads of your parents” (4:6). The proverb promises that formation holds; Lehi is betting that a blessing can be laid down now and collected generations later, which is more than the proverb says and depends on it having said that much.

links.note: “If ye are brought up in the right way that ye should go, ye will not depart from it.” The whole of Proverbs 22:6 is here in order, with the KJV's two distinctive runs intact and only the person changed (he → ye). The 1830 reading is the evidential one: it adds “right” and “that”, and the 1920 edition deleted both, so the modern text reads “brought up in the way ye should go” and is nearer the KJV than the first edition was. That is the same direction of drift recorded at 1 Nephi 1:20 (CONVENTIONS §8) — a later editor tidying the Book of Mormon back toward its source — and it means the borrowing is visible in 1830 despite the tidying, not because of it.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, if ye are cursed, behold, I leave my blessing upon you, that the cursing may be taken from you, and be answered upon the heads of your parents.
Wherefore, because of my blessing, the Lord God will not suffer that ye shall perish; wherefore, he will be merciful unto you, and unto your seed, forever.
And it came to pass that after my father had made an end of speaking to the sons and daughters of Laman, he caused the sons and daughters of Lemuel to be brought before him.

And he spake unto them, saying: Behold, my sons and my daughters, which are the sons and the daughters of my second son; behold, I leave unto you the same blessing which I left unto the sons and daughters of Laman; wherefore, thou shalt not utterly be destroyed; but in the end, thy seed shall be blessed.
And it came to pass that when my father had made an end of speaking unto them, behold, it came to pass that he spake unto the sons of Ishmael, yea, and even all his household.

And after that he had made an end of speaking unto them, he spake unto Sam, saying: Blessed art thou, and thy seed: for thou shalt inherit the land, like unto thy brother, Nephi. And thy seed shall be numbered with his seed; and thou shalt be even like unto thy brother, and thy seed like unto his seed; and thou shalt be blessed in all thy days.

And it came to pass that after Lehi had spake unto all his household, according to the feelings of his heart, and the spirit of the Lord which was in him, he waxed old. And it came to pass that he died, and was buried.

links.text: And when Jacob had made an end of commanding his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the ghost, and was gathered unto his people.

provenance.other: “made an end of” is formulaic — it occurs in exactly 38 KJV verses — so this link rests on the shape of the scene and not on its wording. Genesis 49:33 happens to be one of the 38, and is the one that closes a deathbed blessing. Note that with the pronoun attached, “he died, and was buried” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 2 Chronicles 35:24, Josiah — but that is an artifact of how often the formula takes a named subject instead, and the exclusion register discharges it at this verse.
provenance.significance: Chapters 1-4 of 2 Nephi are a Genesis 49 in full: the father calls his sons, blesses them in birth order, gives the longest and strangest oracle to Joseph (2 Nephi 3, on the Joseph who was carried into Egypt), and then dies. What the Book of Mormon adds is the generation below — Lehi blesses the children of Laman and Lemuel, not Laman and Lemuel — because unlike Jacob he is blessing sons he has already lost. The form is Jacob's; the pathos is the alteration.

links.note: “After Lehi had spake unto all his household, according to the feelings of his heart … he waxed old. And it came to pass that he died, and was buried.” The verbal contact is thin by design: “died, and was buried” occurs in exactly 8 KJV verses and is a chronicler's formula, and “he waxed old” occurs in exactly 0. The case is structural. Genesis 49:33 is the KJV's model for the sentence that ends a patriarchal blessing scene — the blessings finished, the sons dismissed, the patriarch dead in the same breath — and 2 Nephi 1-4 has spent four chapters assembling exactly that scene, down to the Joseph oracle in the emphatic position. Catalogued figural rather than as an allusion because no clause is borrowed; the argument is that the frame is.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that not many days after his death, Laman and Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael, were angry with me, because of the admonitions of the Lord:

links.text: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.

provenance.other: “not many days after” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:13; the nearest other reading is Acts 1:5's “not many days hence”.
provenance.significance: If the phrase is borrowed it brings its parable with it, and the parable is about brothers: the younger goes off with the inheritance and the elder “was angry, and would not go in” (Luke 15:28). 2 Nephi 4:13 is the verse where the elder brothers become angry with the younger who has the birthright, and the family will divide permanently within the chapter. That is the whole plot of Luke 15 read from the elder brother's side.

links.note: “Not many days after his death, Laman and Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael, were angry with me.” The phrase is a KJV singleton, which is why it is recorded at all; the reading it supports is that the sentence which opens the Book of Mormon's permanent fraternal breach opens with the words that open the parable of the two brothers, and pairs them with the elder brother's anger from the end of it.
links.whyNot: “Not many days after” is ordinary narrative connective tissue and its singleton status is an accident of how rarely the KJV needs that transition, not a mark of distinctiveness — the count measures the King James translators' habits, not Luke's vocabulary. Nothing else in the verse touches Luke 15, and the anger is not at 15:13 but fifteen verses later. Recorded at low confidence as a reading worth having on the record, not as a claim of dependence.

pericopes.text: for I, Nephi, was constrained to speak unto them, according to the word. For I had spake many things unto them, and also my father, before his death; many of which sayings, are written upon mine other plates: for a more history part are written upon mine other plates.

And upon these, I write the things of my soul, and many of the Scriptures which are engraven upon the plates of brass: For my soul deliteth in the Scriptures; and my heart pondereth them, and writeth them for the learning and the profit of my children.

links.text: For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.

provenance.other: “written for our learning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 15:4.
provenance.significance: Romans 15:4 is the KJV's charter for reading old scripture in a new situation: whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. Nephi applies it to his own act of writing — he transcribes the plates of brass so that his children may learn — and the psalm that follows immediately is a demonstration of what he means, a lament assembled almost entirely out of the scriptures he has just said he ponders. The verse that licenses the borrowing is itself borrowed.

links.note: “And my heart pondereth them, and writeth them for the learning and the profit of my children.” The KJV's phrase for the purpose of written scripture appears here as the purpose of Nephi's own plates, with “our” replaced by “my children” and “profit” added — the latter is Paul's word two chapters earlier in the same argument and 2 Timothy 3:16's (“profitable for doctrine”). This is the chapter's hinge: verse 15 states a theory of scripture-reading, and verses 16-35 enact it.

links.text: But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.

provenance.other: “pondered them in her heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:19. The KJV uses the verb “ponder” of a person only here and at Luke 2:19's echo in Proverbs 4:26 (“ponder the path of thy feet”); Nephi has both idioms in this chapter, the heart at 4:15-16 and the path at 4:33.
provenance.significance: Mary's pondering is the KJV's one image of a person holding revelation privately because it cannot yet be spoken, and it stands three verses after the shepherds have told everyone. Nephi's is the same posture with the same reason: at 4:25 he has seen things “too great for man” and was “bidden that I should not write them”. The psalm is what a person does with a revelation they are not permitted to publish.

links.note: “My heart pondereth them”, and at 4:16 “my heart pondereth continually upon the things which I have seen and heard.” The KJV's collocation of pondering with the heart is Luke 2:19's alone, and the Book of Mormon has it twice in two verses. Adjudicated at first use; 4:16 is the same borrowing continued and is registered in recurrenceRefs rather than given a second row.

pericopes.text: Behold, my soul delighteth in the things of the Lord; and my heart pondereth continually upon the things which I have seen and heard.

links.text: For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

provenance.other: “the things which we have seen and heard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:20. The bare pair “seen and heard” occurs in exactly 5.
provenance.significance: Acts 4:20 is Peter and John before the Sanhedrin, refusing an order to stop speaking: we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard. Nephi's sentence is the same words under the opposite constraint — he cannot speak them (4:25, “I was bidden that I should not write them”), so he ponders them instead. The apostles' defiance becomes the prophet's silence, and the verse is the pivot into a psalm that is 4:16's suppressed speech finding an outlet.

links.note: “My heart pondereth continually upon the things which I have seen and heard.” The five-word run is a KJV singleton and Nephi keeps it whole, changing only the person. Its force is the change of situation: in Acts the phrase is the reason a man must speak, here it is the content of what a man keeps to himself.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, notwithstanding the great goodness of the Lord, in shewing me his great and marvellous works, my heart exclaimeth, O wretched man that I am; yea, my heart sorroweth, because of my flesh. My soul grieveth, because of mine iniquities.

links.text: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?

provenance.other: “O wretched man that I am” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 7:24, reproduced here word for word. The 1830 spellings elsewhere in the verse — “shewing”, “marvellous” — are the KJV's and were modernized in 1920.
provenance.significance: Recover Romans 7:24's second half and the whole shape of the psalm appears: “who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” Nephi asks that question four times over the next fifteen verses — “because of my flesh” (4:17, 4:27), “my flesh waste away” (4:26), “wilt thou redeem my soul? wilt thou deliver me?” (4:31) — and Romans 7 supplies the terms of each. Romans 7:18, “in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing”; 7:23, “the law of sin which is in my members”, warring and “bringing me into captivity”. The psalm of Nephi is Romans 7:14-25 in the first person, and it resolves the way Paul resolves it, by turning from the flesh to a rock outside it (4:30, 4:35).

links.note: Six words of Romans 7:24, verbatim and in order, from the only KJV verse in which they occur. This is the exclamation the whole psalm is built to make, and it is not decoration: what follows it in Nephi — flesh, iniquity, sin that besets, the desire to rejoice defeated by groaning — is what follows it in Paul, read backwards up the chapter. Note that the borrowing is a New Testament borrowing placed in the mouth of a writer the text dates to about 570 BC, and that the surrounding sentence is the Book of Mormon's own; Nephi does not quote Romans, he speaks in it.

pericopes.text: I am encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins which doth so easily beset me.

links.text: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,

provenance.other: “which doth so easily beset” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:1. “Encompassed about” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; the KJV reads “compassed about”, which occurs in exactly 5, one of them Hebrews 12:1 itself. So the Book of Mormon has the singleton clause exactly and the common clause inexactly, which is the signature of quotation from memory rather than transcription.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12 is not merely quarried here, it is followed. 12:1 gives 2 Nephi 4:18 the sin that so easily besets; 12:12's drooping hands and feeble knees give 4:28-29 their “no longer droop” and “do not slacken my strength”; 12:13's “make straight paths” gives 4:33 “wilt thou make my path straight before me”. Three verses of one paragraph, in the source's order, spread across the psalm's turn from despair to petition — which is the turn Hebrews 12 itself makes. The catalogue's 1 Nephi 4:2 entry found the same habit with Hebrews 11: the Book of Mormon uses a chapter of Hebrews as an index and works down it.

links.note: “The sins which doth so easily beset me.” The clause is Hebrews 12:1's, singular for plural and me for us, and even the KJV's ungrammatical singular verb survives — “the sins which DOTH so easily beset” — which is the tell, since a writer composing freely would have written “do”. The 1920 edition left it standing. “Encompassed about” in the same sentence is Hebrews 12:1's “compassed about” loosened; the pairing of the two clauses is Hebrews' and nobody else's.

pericopes.text: And when I desire to rejoice, my heart groaneth because of my sins; nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted.

links.text: For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.

provenance.other: “I know whom I have believed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 1:12. The Book of Mormon substitutes “trusted” for “believed” and adds the preposition: “I know in whom I have trusted.”
provenance.significance: The substitution is the interesting part, because it sets up the end of the psalm. 2 Timothy's verb is belief; Nephi's is trust, and trust is what 4:34 will spend a whole verse on — “I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever … cursed is he that putteth his trust in man.” The verse that steadies him in the middle of the lament is Paul's confidence with Jeremiah's vocabulary dropped into it, sixteen verses before Jeremiah arrives.

links.note: “Nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted.” The KJV has this sentence once, in a chapter about not being ashamed under affliction, and the Book of Mormon's “nevertheless” answers 2 Timothy 1:12's “nevertheless I am not ashamed” in the same position. Catalogued as paraphrase rather than quotation because the governing verb is changed; the syntax, the concessive, and the argumentative function are unaltered.

pericopes.text: My God hath been my support; he hath led me through mine afflictions in the wilderness; and he hath preserved me upon the waters of the great deep.

links.text: He hath led me, and brought me into darkness, but not into light.

provenance.other: “He hath led me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:2, and “he hath filled me with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:15 — the two openings of 2 Nephi 4:20 and 4:21. Both are within fourteen verses of each other in one passage.
provenance.significance: Lamentations 3:1-16 is the KJV's only sustained first-person catalogue of what God has done TO a man, sixteen verses of “He hath led me”, “He hath filled me”, “he hath hedged me about”, “he hath made my chain heavy”. 2 Nephi 4:20-25 is six verses of the same anaphora with the sign reversed: he hath led me THROUGH mine afflictions, he hath PRESERVED me, he hath filled me WITH HIS LOVE, he hath heard my cry.
